name: Swoop (ex-Swoop jets flown by WestJet)
description: Swoop's scheme, still on its 737-800s and 737 MAX 8s now flying for WestJet after Swoop was folded into it in 2024: a white fuselage with 'swoop' in huge pink script-like lower case over the forward windows, a small pink airplane at its front, and 'WESTJET' with its maple leaf small under it (added since); the fin pink with a big white swoosh curling up from its root and a small white airplane near the tip, the pink carried forward along the dorsal fillet; white engines; pink winglets.

areas.name: the white swoosh: from the root's front, sweeping aft and up, then curling forward to a point under the tip

logos.description: Swoop's small airplane glyph, a simple top-view jet pointing up the fin, white near the tip.
The same airplane glyph in pink, flying at the front of the 'swoop' title on the right side; on the left it follows the 'p' (toward the tail).
The airplane glyph after the title's 'p' on the left side.
A small Canadian flag after the registration over the rear windows, 'Proudly' over it.

titles.style: Swoop's wordmark: huge, heavy, rounded pink lower case with a swash look, from behind the forward door to over the wing's root, its tops nearly at the crown and its 'p' dropping below the windows.
WestJet's wordmark small, with its teal maple leaf ahead of it and 'Proudly operated by / Fièrement exploité par' above, under the title's middle: added when Swoop was folded in.

notes: Swoop (WSW) was folded into WestJet in October 2024; its jets fly on as WestJet in Swoop's paint, with a small 'Proudly operated by WESTJET' added (on the 2026 photos, not the 2024 one), until repainted. Drawn on C-GISM (right side, climbing, 2026-03-09), fitted to the measured 737 MAX 8 shape and checked on C-GYLP the same day; the left side's layout from C-GNDG (737-800, 2024). The fin's swoosh is a smooth area (it's drawn as a curve, a logo-like shape, not a stripe); the dorsal fillet is pink. The title's letters are huge and interlocked: set as text it can only approximate the wordmark, which is why it names a mark. The airplane glyph's place on the left side is from the 2024 photo of a -800 (low).
